results.title: Neuron characterisation
results.question: What is known about the LPLC2 visual neuron type? Where is it, what does it connect to, and what is its function?
results.response: Information about the LPLC2 visual neuron type is available. The LPLC2 visual neuron type is known to detect looming (expansion) stimuli and elicit a jump escape response. According to the evidence, it has a distinct dendritic arbor in each lobula plate layer, extending outwards from the main fiber in the direction of motion detection for the layer, as described by Klapoetke et al., 2017. This arrangement allows it to detect looming (expansion) stimuli, as reported by Klapoetke et al., 2017. Its activity elicits a jump escape response, as found by Wu et al., 2016, and Klapoetke et al., 2017. VFB holds data on the LPLC2 visual neuron type, including its role as a lobula plate-lobula columnar neuron. VFB does not currently hold detailed data on the specific connections of the LPLC2 visual neuron type beyond its general characterization.

VFB holds data on neurons with some part in the visual system, with [1046](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047735,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in visual system") records, as well as neurons with synaptic terminals, presynaptic terminals, and postsynaptic terminals in the visual system, with [982](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047735,NeuronsSynaptic "Run in VFB: Neurons with synaptic terminals in visual system"), [690](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047735,NeuronsPresynapticHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with presynaptic terminals in visual system"), and [889](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047735,NeuronsPostsynapticHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with postsynaptic terminals in visual system") records, respectively. Additionally, VFB has annotated [1153](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047735,PartsOf "Run in VFB: Parts of visual system") parts of the visual system. However, the exact number of distinct neuron types currently classified within the adult Drosophila visual system and their hierarchical organization is not specified in the available data. To further investigate the classification and organization of neuron types in the visual system, you can explore the VFB data on neurons with some part in the visual system and their synaptic terminals.

results.title: Connectivity strength comparison
results.question: Which neuron type provides the strongest synaptic input to the MBON-gamma1pedc>a/b neuron, and how does this compare to the next strongest inputs?
results.response:
The strongest synaptic input to MBON-gamma1pedc>a/b is from mushroom body intrinsic neurons, and the next strongest input is from Kenyon cells, as indicated by the total weights of 45838 and 44880, respectively, according to VFB data from the VFB query. 

To further investigate the connectivity of MBON-gamma1pedc>a/b, VFB holds data on its downstream and upstream connectivity classes, with [2788](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for MBON") and [2077](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for MBON") records, respectively. Additionally, VFB has annotated [157](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in MBON") records of transgene expression in mushroom body output neurons, which may provide more insight into their function and connectivity. 

For more detailed information on the specific neuron types and their connections, the user can explore the available data on subclasses of mushroom body output neurons, scRNAseq data, and images of MBON.

results.title: Shared connectivity
results.question: Do the alpha/beta and gamma Kenyon cells converge on any of the same downstream MBON types? Which MBONs receive input from both?
results.response: The connectome data indicates that alpha/beta Kenyon cells and gamma Kenyon cells converge on the same [mushroom body output neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047953 "Open mushroom body output neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") types. VFB records show that some mushroom body output neurons receive input from both alpha/beta Kenyon cells and gamma Kenyon cells. Specifically, VFB found 13 shared downstream target classes among the compared source classes, including mushroom body output neuron 32 and mushroom body output neuron 29. VFB has annotated downstream connectivity classes for both alpha/beta Kenyon cells and gamma Kenyon cells, with [366](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00100248,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for KCab") and [491](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00100248,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for KCab") upstream connectivity classes for alpha/beta Kenyon cells, and VFB holds data on transgene expression and scRNAseq for both cell types. The user can explore the specific connectivity patterns by querying the downstream connectivity classes for alpha/beta Kenyon cells and gamma Kenyon cells, and the upstream connectivity classes for mushroom body output neurons.

results.title: Anatomical containment chain
results.question: Trace the anatomical containment hierarchy from the DA1 glomerulus up to the top-level brain structure. What is each level in the hierarchy?
results.response:
The anatomical containment hierarchy from the [antennal lobe glomerulus DA1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003932 "Open antennal lobe glomerulus DA1 in Virtual Fly Brain") up to the top-level brain structure, as recorded in VFB, is: antennal lobe glomerulus DA1 -> adult antennal lobe -> adult deutocerebrum -> adult cerebrum -> adult central brain -> adult brain. 

VFB holds various data related to antennal lobe glomerulus DA1, including [10](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003932,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1") records of neurons with some part in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1, 10 records of neurons with synaptic terminals in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1, and [911](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003932,ImagesNeurons "Run in VFB: Images of neurons with some part in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1") images of neurons with some part in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1. 

To further explore the hierarchy and related data, you can query VFB for more information on the adult antennal lobe, adult deutocerebrum, adult cerebrum, adult central brain, and adult brain, as well as investigate the available neuron and image data for antennal lobe glomerulus DA1.

results.title: Cross-region connectivity
results.question: What neuron types connect the central complex to the lateral accessory lobe, and how strong are these connections?
results.response:
The neuron types that connect the [adult central complex](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003632 "Open adult central complex in Virtual Fly Brain") to the [lateral accessory lobe on L3 CNS template, Wood2018](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_00050314 "Open lateral accessory lobe on L3 CNS template, Wood2018 in Virtual Fly Brain") include larval mushroom body output neurons, such as c2, f2, and m1, as well as larval dopaminergic neurons, like DM1b, according to VFB. Additionally, VFB records show other neuron types connecting the central complex to the lateral accessory lobe, including PFL1, PFL2_PB4, PFL3_PB7, PFL1_PB1, PFL1_PB7, and PFL1_PB2, as found by the VFB query.

VFB holds numerous records of neurons with some part in, or synaptic terminals in, both the adult central complex and the lateral accessory lobe on L3 CNS template, Wood2018. For example, VFB has annotated [363](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003632,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in adult central complex") neurons with some part in the adult central complex and [8](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=VFB_00050314,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in embryonic/larval lateral accessory lobe") neurons with some part in the embryonic/larval lateral accessory lobe. 

The strength of these connections is not explicitly stated in the available evidence. To further investigate the connectivity and strength of connections between the adult central complex and the lateral accessory lobe on L3 CNS template, Wood2018, you can explore the available images of neurons, tracts, and transgene expression in these regions, which are listed in the available VFB data.

results.title: Experimental planning
results.question: I want to study the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance in Drosophila. What neurons are involved, how are they connected, and what genetic tools can I use to access them?
results.response:
To study the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance in Drosophila, you would need to identify the specific neurons involved in this behavior. VFB does not currently hold data on the exact neurons involved in CO2 avoidance. 

The connectome data may indicate which neurons are connected and potentially involved in this behavior, but without specific data on CO2 avoidance, it is unclear which neurons to focus on. 

Genetic tools such as GAL4 drivers and split-GAL4 drivers can be used to access specific neurons, but without knowing which neurons are involved in CO2 avoidance, it is difficult to recommend specific tools. 

You can query the VFB database for neurons that have been annotated with terms related to CO2 sensing or avoidance, and then explore the connectome data to see how these neurons are connected. You can also look for publications that have studied CO2 avoidance in Drosophila and see if they have identified specific neurons or genetic tools that can be used to study this behavior. 

VFB holds data on various neurons and their connections, as well as genetic tools that can be used to access these neurons. You can search the VFB database for neurons and genetic tools that may be relevant to your study.

results.title: Complete neuron profile
results.question: Give me a comprehensive profile of the giant fiber neuron: its anatomy, connectivity, available driver lines, and relevant publications.
results.response:
The [giant fiber neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004020 "Open giant fiber neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") is a large adult descending neuron that controls jump escape behavior, as stated by Thomas and Wyman (1984). VFB records show that the giant fiber neuron has a distinct anatomy and connectivity. 

VFB holds [22](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of DNp01") records of images of the giant fiber neuron, specifically DNp01, as well as [14](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in DNp01") records of transgene expression in DNp01. The connectome data indicates that DNp01 has [361](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for DNp01") downstream connectivity classes and [435](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for DNp01") upstream connectivity classes. 

The giant fiber neuron is associated with certain GAL4 drivers, which can be used to study its expression pattern. VFB has annotated data on the expression pattern of the giant fiber neuron, which can be used to inform the selection of driver lines for experimental studies.

For more information on the giant fiber neuron, including its anatomy, connectivity, and available driver lines, the user can query VFB for specific details, such as transgene expression patterns or downstream and upstream connectivity classes. Relevant publications, including the study by Thomas and Wyman (1984), can provide further insight into the role of the giant fiber neuron in jump escape behavior.

results.title: Hypothesis generation
results.question: Based on connectivity data, what neuron types might mediate a connection between the visual system and the mushroom body? Could visual information reach the memory circuit?
results.response: Based on the connectivity data, neuron types such as [ML-VPN2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052139 "Open ML-VPN2 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mt-VPN1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052141 "Open Mt-VPN1 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mt-VPN](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052140 "Open Mt-VPN in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mti](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052142 "Open Mti in Virtual Fly Brain"), [T4ai neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052241 "Open T4ai neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") might mediate a connection between the [visual system](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047735 "Open visual system in Virtual Fly Brain") and the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain"), as indicated by VFB. Additionally, VFB records show that adult visual projection neurons, which have presynaptic terminals in the mushroom body, could also mediate this connection, as described by Vogt et al., 2016. The connectome data indicates that there are neurons with presynaptic terminals in both the visual system and the mushroom body, suggesting a potential pathway for visual information to reach the memory circuit. VFB holds records of [1046](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047735,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in visual system") neurons with some part in the visual system and [602](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in mushroom body") neurons with some part in the mushroom body, as well as records of neurons with synaptic terminals in both systems, which could be relevant for understanding this potential connection. To further investigate this connection, one could explore the specific neuron types and tracts that innervate both the visual system and the mushroom body, such as the [adult optic lobe-calycal tract](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00048333 "Open adult optic lobe-calycal tract in Virtual Fly Brain").

results.title: Novel circuit exploration
results.question: What is the connectivity between thermosensory neurons and the mushroom body? Could temperature information influence memory formation?
results.response:
The connectivity between thermosensory neurons and the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") is indicated by VFB downstream class-connectivity previews for adult thermosensory projection neurons, which include mushroom-body-associated dopaminergic neurons and gamma main Kenyon cells when available, as recorded in VFB. VFB holds [430](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005918,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for thermosensory neuron") records of downstream connectivity classes for [thermosensory neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005918 "Open thermosensory neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") and [602](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in mushroom body") records of neurons with some part in mushroom body. 

VFB records show that thermosensory projection neurons relay temperature-detecting neurons to higher brain centers. Given the connection between thermosensory neurons and the mushroom body, it is possible that temperature information could influence memory formation, as the mushroom body is known to be involved in memory and learning processes. However, the exact nature of this influence is not specified in the available VFB data. 

To further investigate this question, one could explore the specific downstream connectivity classes for thermosensory neuron and the neurons with some part in mushroom body, as well as the expression patterns overlapping mushroom body, all of which are available in VFB.
